newsitem.title: ITALY: Employers reject Italy govt metalworker peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Employers reject Italy govt metalworker peace plan.

text.p: Employers group Federmeccanica reaffirmed on Tuesday that it would not accept a government proposal aimed at ending the long running pay dispute in the Italian metalworkers and engineering sector.

Federmeccanica director general, Michele Figurati, told reporters after a meeting of the federation that negotiations were blocked and called on the trades unions to lower their demands for a pay hike.

The government has suggested management offer workers a monthly pay rise of 200,000 lire per month for the two-year contract. Unions, which wanted 230,000 lire, accepted the proposal, but management has stuck to its 139,000 lire offer.

"At this moment, there are no negotations, and I don't know when they will be unblocked," Figurati said. "We won't deal on the basis of (the government suggestion). The cost has to be lower," he added.
Federmeccanica chairman, Albertini Gabriele, said the organisation was united in rejecting the government plan.
"An objective of this meeting was to show that we weren't divided," he said.
He said the government proposals would cost industry an estimated 15 trillion lire and added that Federmeccanica had planned for the wage deal to cost 9.8 trillion lire.
"The difference between those two figures is the object of the negotiations," he said.
The employers group's Figurati stressed that management was prepared to return to the negotiating table. "We are open to talks to find a solution," he said.
Federmeccanica said one of its aims was to agree with unions on a lower pay deal for firms in the depressed south of the country.
In a statement, the federation said it had told its team of negotiators to: "take every effort to reach a deal which is compatible with the economic reality of the sector".

Leaders of the three major unions in the sector, the Fim-Fiom-Uilm, are due to meet on Wednesday. They have already called two eight-hour stoppages and last week initiated a further wave of strike action.

Union leaders said they would concentrate their efforts on large industrial groups while the main union federations have threatened to stage a general strike in support of the metal and engineering workers.
The dispute, which has been dragging on since last June, centres on the interpretation of a landmark 1993 wage deal which scrapped automatic index-linked wage increases.
Unions say the deal allows for a full catch-up between past government forecasts, on which the two-year contracts are based, and actual price rises.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government said its proposals were within the spirit of the 1993 accord, something rejected by management which said the suggestions were inflationary. -- Rome newsroom +396 6782501
